variants.title: Run the candidate loop
variants.context: Every candidate goes through the same four steps: freeze the decision and its evaluation slice, build a simple baseline, add one mechanism at a time, then compare on identical evidence. A mechanism is kept only when the measured gain justifies the failure surface it adds.
variants.prompt: A policy assistant invents policy details and the team wants to know whether retrieval fixes it. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Add authorized retrieval as the single change under test.
Score both runs on the same cases for task success, tokens, latency, and cost.
Freeze the user outcome, the evaluation slice, the constraints, and the cost of a wrong answer.
Run the shortest viable prompt with no tools as the deterministic baseline.
Keep retrieval only if the measured gain justifies the new failure surface it introduces.

variants.hint: What has to be frozen before any two runs can be compared?
variants.explanation: Frame, baseline, one mechanism, then compare on identical evidence. The baseline is what exposes which capability is actually missing.

variants.title: Run the candidate loop
variants.context: Every candidate goes through the same four steps: freeze the decision and its evaluation slice, build a simple baseline, add one mechanism at a time, then compare on identical evidence. A mechanism is kept only when the measured gain justifies the failure surface it adds.
variants.prompt: An engineer wants to justify routing a triage workflow from the balanced tier to the deliberate tier. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Route to the deliberate tier only where the gain is measured, and preserve the known-good fallback.
Fix one prompt, one evidence set, and one success definition that both tiers must be judged against.
Record the current balanced-tier route as the control run.
Compare task success on the critical slice against the added latency and cost.
Change only the model tier and leave the prompt, tools, and evidence untouched.

variants.hint: How many things may change between the control and the candidate?
variants.explanation: A tier upgrade is justified by incremental task success on the target slice, measured against incremental latency and cost, never by the tier label.

variants.title: Run the candidate loop
variants.context: Every candidate goes through the same four steps: freeze the decision and its evaluation slice, build a simple baseline, add one mechanism at a time, then compare on identical evidence. A mechanism is kept only when the measured gain justifies the failure surface it adds.
variants.prompt: A candidate added a bounded tool call and a longer prompt at the same time, and quality moved. Put the steps in order that recovers a defensible comparison.

items.text: Attribute the quality change to one mechanism and keep only the one that earns its failure surface.
Return to the baseline prompt with no tools and measure it again.
Reintroduce the longer prompt alone and measure it against that baseline.
Restate the frozen outcome, slice, and constraints the comparison has to hold fixed.
Reintroduce the bounded tool alone and measure it against the same baseline.

variants.hint: Two changes at once leave you with how many attributable results?
variants.explanation: Adding one mechanism at a time is what makes a result attributable. Bundled changes hide which one paid for the extra failure surface.

variants.title: Route a governed request
variants.context: The model is one dependency inside a control system. Each request binds identity and deadline, assembles permission-filtered evidence, generates or proposes under a tier, token, schema, and tool ceiling, then verifies structure, citations, safety, and authorization before returning text or committing a side effect.
variants.prompt: An employee asks a policy question that must be answered with citations. Put the request stages in order.

items.text: Apply permission filters, then retrieve evidence and preserve its source identifiers.
Validate structure, citations, and safety before any text reaches the user.
Generate under the selected tier, token ceiling, output schema, and retry limit.
Bind the tenant, user, intent, deadline, rate limit, and request identifier to the request.

variants.hint: At which stage is permission decided?
variants.explanation: Identity and permission filtering come before retrieval, and verification comes before release. Every stage emits a typed result and a trace.

variants.title: Route a governed request
variants.context: The model is one dependency inside a control system. Each request binds identity and deadline, assembles permission-filtered evidence, generates or proposes under a tier, token, schema, and tool ceiling, then verifies structure, citations, safety, and authorization before returning text or committing a side effect.
variants.prompt: A request will commit a refund, which is a real side effect. Put the stages in order, ending with the commit.

items.text: Let the model propose a refund tool call from the allowed tool list.
Assemble only the account records that this identity is permitted to see.
Validate the arguments and confirm the requesting identity may perform that refund.
Capture the requesting identity, deadline, data classification, and request identifier.
Commit once under an idempotency key, then record the route, versions, and gate verdicts.

variants.hint: Between proposing an action and performing it, what has to happen?
variants.explanation: A model-generated tool call is a proposal. Deterministic authorization bound to the requesting identity, plus argument validation and idempotency, stands between the proposal and the side effect.

variants.title: Route a governed request
variants.context: The model is one dependency inside a control system. Each request binds identity and deadline, assembles permission-filtered evidence, generates or proposes under a tier, token, schema, and tool ceiling, then verifies structure, citations, safety, and authorization before returning text or committing a side effect.
variants.prompt: No authorized source supports the question that was asked. Put the stages in order, ending with the declared outcome.

items.text: Apply permission filters, then search the authorized policy sources.
Return the declared insufficient-evidence outcome and trace which gate ended the request.
Skip generation rather than answering from missing or unauthorized sources.
Bind the request identity, intent, and deadline before any search runs.
Record that the required evidence is absent and stop the context stage.

variants.hint: What does the contract promise when the evidence is not there?
variants.explanation: Insufficient evidence is a declared, typed outcome, not a fallback to the model's own knowledge. The trace must name the gate that ended the request.

variants.title: Budget one request
variants.context: Budget one request before estimating the fleet. Cost per request is input tokens times the input rate plus output tokens times the output rate, all divided by one million. Planning latency is the fixed stages plus first token plus output tokens divided by output tokens per second, and the concurrency floor is requests per second times the seconds one request lasts.
variants.prompt: Planning stages cost 120 ms at the gateway, 190 ms for retrieval, and 85 ms for safety. The tier returns a first token in 520 ms and then produces 240 output tokens at 120 tokens per second. What is the planning latency?
variants.hint: Generation time is output tokens divided by the token rate, and it is only one term of three.
variants.explanation: Planning latency is fixed stages plus first token plus generation: 395 plus 520 plus 2,000 gives 2,915 ms. It is an estimate, not an SLO proof.

mistakes.feedback: You left out generation time; 240 tokens at 120 per second take two full seconds.
You dropped the fixed stages; gateway, retrieval, and safety add 395 ms before the model starts.

variants.title: Budget one request
variants.context: Budget one request before estimating the fleet. Cost per request is input tokens times the input rate plus output tokens times the output rate, all divided by one million. Planning latency is the fixed stages plus first token plus output tokens divided by output tokens per second, and the concurrency floor is requests per second times the seconds one request lasts.
variants.prompt: A compact-tier route uses 1,600 input tokens priced at $0.25 per million and 400 output tokens priced at $2 per million. What do 1,000 such requests cost in dollars?
variants.hint: Price the two token classes separately, then scale the single-request figure.
variants.explanation: One request costs (1,600 times 0.25 plus 400 times 2) divided by 1,000,000, which is $0.0012, so a thousand requests cost $1.20.

mistakes.feedback: You priced all 2,000 tokens at the output rate; input and output bill at different rates.
That is the cost of one request; the question asks for a thousand of them.

variants.title: Budget one request
variants.context: Budget one request before estimating the fleet. Cost per request is input tokens times the input rate plus output tokens times the output rate, all divided by one million. Planning latency is the fixed stages plus first token plus output tokens divided by output tokens per second, and the concurrency floor is requests per second times the seconds one request lasts.
variants.prompt: A route is planned at 90 requests per minute and each request occupies a worker for 4 seconds. What concurrency floor should capacity planning assume?
variants.hint: The formula needs traffic expressed per second, not per minute.
variants.explanation: The concurrency floor is requests per second times request seconds: 1.5 times 4 gives 6 workers busy at once. Queueing and retries push the real number higher.

mistakes.feedback: You multiplied requests per minute by seconds; convert traffic to requests per second first.
You divided traffic by the request duration; a longer request needs more concurrency, not less.

variants.title: Defend the release
variants.context: Hold or narrow a release when its evidence cannot be defended: representative evaluation is missing, a critical slice fails, required data cannot be authorized, a model or tool holds more authority than the user, the safe fallback is untested, or operators cannot identify and roll back the active versions.
variants.prompt: A candidate lifts aggregate task success from 88 to 92 percent, but the Spanish-language slice falls from 90 to 71 percent. The team proposes shipping because the weighted score improved. What should happen?
options: Hold the release for that slice, because a healthy average must not cancel a failed critical slice.
Ship it, because the weighted aggregate is the release metric the team agreed to use.
Ship it and add the Spanish slice to next month's monitoring once traffic confirms the drop.
optionFeedback: Slice evidence exists so that one aggregate cannot hide a population that got measurably worse.
One weighted score is not a release gate; a failed critical slice is not cancelled by a better mean.
Monitoring after release makes users the test population for a regression already measured offline.
variants.hint: What is an aggregate score able to hide?
variants.explanation: Do not collapse every criterion into one weighted score. A failed critical slice blocks the release on its own.

variants.title: Defend the release
variants.context: Hold or narrow a release when its evidence cannot be defended: representative evaluation is missing, a critical slice fails, required data cannot be authorized, a model or tool holds more authority than the user, the safe fallback is untested, or operators cannot identify and roll back the active versions.
variants.prompt: A candidate has passed offline replay and two weeks of shadow traffic with no user-visible effects. The team wants it on every request Monday. What is the defensible next step?
options: Release to everyone, since shadow traffic already ran the candidate on real production requests.
Keep shadowing for another month until the sample is large enough to settle the difference.
Expose a small eligible cohort with a spend cap, a kill switch, and a named owner who may expand or stop it.
optionFeedback: Shadow runs produce no user-visible effects, so they never test what happens when users act on the output.
More shadow traffic still never exercises user-visible behavior, side effects, or the kill switch.
Canary with limits is the step between shadow and full release, and it needs a predeclared owner.
variants.hint: Which release step is the first one real users can feel?
variants.explanation: Replay, then shadow, then a limited canary with a kill switch and a named owner. Each step tests something the previous one could not.

variants.title: Defend the release
variants.context: Hold or narrow a release when its evidence cannot be defended: representative evaluation is missing, a critical slice fails, required data cannot be authorized, a model or tool holds more authority than the user, the safe fallback is untested, or operators cannot identify and roll back the active versions.
variants.prompt: An incident review finds that operators cannot tell which prompt and index versions served a failing request. Quality, safety, and latency gates all passed. What follows?
options: Hold or narrow the release until traces name the active versions and a rollback target.
Continue the rollout, because the quality, safety, and latency gates all produced passing evidence.
Continue and reconstruct the versions from deploy timestamps if another incident occurs later.
optionFeedback: A release you cannot identify is a release you cannot roll back, which is a stop condition by itself.
Passing gates do not restore the ability to identify and reverse the configuration that is live.
Deploy timestamps do not prove which prompt, route, or index snapshot handled one specific request.
variants.hint: What has to be true before a rollback is even possible?
variants.explanation: Traces must name the model, prompt, route, sources, tools, policies, and configuration versions. Without that, no operator can roll the release back.

variants.title: Sort the evidence
variants.context: A complete evaluation measures four evidence families: task evidence for completion and grounding, safety evidence for policy and injection failures, operational evidence for latency, tokens, and cost, and slice evidence for populations that one aggregate can hide.
variants.prompt: An evaluation report lists four result blocks. Match each block to the evidence family it belongs to.

pairs.label: Task evidence
pairs.detail: Required-fact coverage, grounded citations, and structured-output validity

pairs.label: Safety evidence
pairs.detail: Prompt injection, sensitive-data disclosure, and unauthorized tool attempts

pairs.label: Operational evidence
pairs.detail: p95 stage latency, tokens, cost per successful task, and fallback rate

pairs.label: Slice evidence
pairs.detail: Results split by intent, language, modality, customer tier, and risk level

variants.hint: Ask what each number would let you refuse a release for.
variants.explanation: The four families answer different questions, so none of them substitutes for another. An operational win never settles a safety or slice result.

variants.title: Sort the evidence
variants.context: A complete evaluation measures four evidence families: task evidence for completion and grounding, safety evidence for policy and injection failures, operational evidence for latency, tokens, and cost, and slice evidence for populations that one aggregate can hide.
variants.prompt: A second report adds four more measurements. Match each measurement to the evidence family it belongs to.

pairs.label: Task evidence
pairs.detail: Human preference scores on completed answers against the current baseline

pairs.label: Safety evidence
pairs.detail: Harmful refusals and unsafe compliance counted on adversarial cases

pairs.label: Operational evidence
pairs.detail: Timeout rate, retry rate, queue depth, and provider error counts

pairs.label: Slice evidence
pairs.detail: Failure rate broken out by document type and by selected model route

variants.hint: Two of these count failures of behavior and two count failures of the path.
variants.explanation: Safety evidence covers both directions of failure, harmful compliance and harmful refusal. Slice evidence re-cuts any result by a population an average would smooth over.

variants.title: Sort the evidence
variants.context: A complete evaluation measures four evidence families: task evidence for completion and grounding, safety evidence for policy and injection failures, operational evidence for latency, tokens, and cost, and slice evidence for populations that one aggregate can hide.
variants.prompt: Four symptoms are reported after a release. Match each symptom to the evidence family that should have caught it.

pairs.label: Task evidence
pairs.detail: Answers stopped citing the paragraph that actually supports the claim

pairs.label: Safety evidence
pairs.detail: An instruction pasted into a document changed the assistant's behavior

pairs.label: Operational evidence
pairs.detail: The p99 stage time doubled once the prompt template grew

pairs.label: Slice evidence
pairs.detail: Aggregate success held steady while one customer tier got worse

variants.hint: For each symptom, ask which family runs the test that would have failed first.
variants.explanation: Every production symptom should map back to a family in the evaluation set. A symptom with no owning family is a gap in the evaluation, not bad luck.
